lines: PRESIDENT:  Good morning to all of you.  Before we
commence the evidentiary hearing we have an
application from the respondent, which only received
thanks to my co-arbitrator forwarding it to me this
morning.  So I did not have time to respond to it, but
I would like to invite claimant, if -- did claimant
receive it when it was sent?
MR HAUGENEDER:  We received it, I believe I read it,
I read it this morning at breakfast -- like you,
probably.
PRESIDENT:  Do you have any comment or you would like to
raise?  Please go ahead.
MR HAUGENEDER:  We object against this application in the
strongest terms.  This is new evidence and the
respondent says it is relevant new evidence.  We don't
know what it is.  We had no opportunity to talk about
with the witness that is concerned, Ms Measic.  We
could not address that in any of our submissions.
This is the chain of messages, apparently over a long
period of time, one and a half years.  So that could
not have been hidden somewhere and discovered only
yesterday evening by accident.
Mr Barash has submitted two witness statements,
one dated 21 November 2024, the other dated
17 September 2025.  And in his witness statement, he
talks about the relationship with PPD.
Now, in any witness interview, these WhatsApp
messages must have come up.  This is not something
hidden.  There must have been -- there were apparently
many messages to which he wants to refer.  This must
have been planned for Mr Barash that these messages
exist.  And if Gazprom had wanted to introduce them,
there was ample opportunity to do that.
Apart from the submissions where that should have
been introduced, we had offered to the respondent to
exchange any new documents that could not have been
produced before on 27 February.  That was rejected by
the respondent.
The respondent then produced on 7 March, 33 new
documents, to which we objected, but which were
admitted.  And now comes this surprise evidence at the
very last hour before the testimony of Ms Measic.  We
couldn't talk to her about it.  We don't know what it
is.  It will be a surprise to her.  It will be
a complete surprise to us.
This is almost a caricature of an ambush.  This is
an ambush.  If this is admitted, we have no
opportunity to make any observations, let alone
reasonable observations, sufficient opportunity to
address that as is required by paragraph 22 of
procedural order number 1.
There is one other point that concerns us very
much.
I would like to show the transcript of yesterday.
That is Mr Talanov's opening statement.
PRESIDENT:  Is this point related to the application?
Right.
MR HAUGENEDER:  And you will see here, he said:
"The parties had thousands of ways to
communicate."
PRESIDENT:  For the record, can you indicate the page
number and the line, please?
MR HAUGENEDER:  Yes.  That is page 183 and the lines are
16 to 20.  Thank you.  And I'm reading it out:
"The parties had thousands of ways to communicate.
Many of the employees knew each other.  Many of people
were communicating on WhatsApp and other messengers.
Silence.  Then you receive the letter signed without
any other additional reservation."
So that's what he said.  So he knew.  He must have
known.  There is no WhatsApp message on the record.
So Mr Talanov knew well yesterday when he made that
submission that these WhatsApp messages existed.
The conclusion from this is that the respondent
has deliberately held back these communications to
ambush us, and we are left wondering whether this is
one of the pressure points that were found by
Dr Goeth.
Thank you.  We object against the admission of --
PRESIDENT:  The objection is heard, and we have heard
also the comments you have made.  I would like to
invite respondent, if there is any reply you would
like to make, and then we will make a decision.
MR TALANOV:  Thank you.  Thank you, dear members of the
panel, members of the tribunal.
Well, from the tone of my message, you saw that
this is very embarrassing situation for us as well.
And we understand that indeed, the parties here need
to secure everything necessary for the due process and
for the other party not to be prejudiced.  So we fully
share many of the concerns raised.
However, as explained, the communication was found
by the witness in the archive and Mr Barash will be
speaking here, he can better comment on the technical
details of how it works.
And as said, it's a fairly short document of maybe
three, four pages, though the period may be long, but
these are very short messages, apparently.  And what
it shows is that there was a parallel track of
correspondence between the parties.  That is not on
the record.  We only see the official letters, but
that is the parallel track that is important.
Unfortunately, none of the parties provided that.
And importantly, both parties have this
correspondence because it is not the document that the
respondent had and somehow was hiding, because that is
the correspondence between the two witnesses.  They
will be speaking in front of the tribunal.
And in any case, that is our duty before the
tribunal and our duty before the client, to inform
about the existence of these documents and to act
openly and not to effectively use the information from
that document against the witness in cross-examination
or employ other tactics.  Therefore, we tried to be
most transparent and most open as possible.
We understand that the other party needs to have
all the chances to review, comment.  We are happy to
share this document with the other parties should they
not have it.  That's why we did not yet seek to put
this document on record, but we asked for instructions
how to proceed best, before we file any formal
application.
And we strongly believe that the other party --
we're happy to share this document -- may have a look
at it, and then we decide how to proceed best, so that
the other party has enough time to review it and
comment it.
But once the tribunal sees the contents of the
document, you will necessarily feel that this document
may be very relevant for the assessment of the
evidence by both witnesses, and it may be in the best
interests of the dispute and the parties to have it on
the record.
So we are ready to go for any procedural
guarantees so that the other party and their witnesses
have chances to comment on this fairly short document
of, as I said, less than five pages.
And we are therefore ready even maybe to make some
concessions on our time and sense of cross-examination
if needed, and the witness to give later
clarifications if the witness and the other party
deems needed, so that no due process concerns would be
present.
And as for the comment on the transcript, indeed,
and that's exactly what I meant and I was saying, and
that is also one of the questions that we requested
the witnesses to consider while preparing.  And that
is how the document and this correspondence came to
our knowledge, while Mr Barash was preparing for the
cross-examination and recollecting the evidence.
At first, when we met with him, he did not -- he
claims not to have seen it or he did not locate it in
the phone.  But it's better for Mr Barash to address
all these technicalities.
And therefore, once he located it, that was done.
But indeed there are other there were other WhatsApp
messages exchanged by the parties known to us, what
they're referring to.  And there are other witnesses
and there are other people referred to in the witness
statements, including Mr Mazilov, for instance.
And therefore this reference to WhatsApp should
not be read as solely limited to WhatsApp
communications with Mr Barash, given that WhatsApp is
a universally used messenger these days.
So we strongly believe that given that this
document originates from both parties, both parties
have it and both witnesses actually were participating
in this correspondence, provided that the parties and
the witnesses have time to comment on a fairly short
document, we may develop some sort of a protocol so
that this document is seen by the tribunal.  Thank
you.
PRESIDENT:  I have a question.  At which point in time
did respondent became aware of the existence of this
document?
MR TALANOV:  That happened yesterday at about 8.40,
Mr Barash called me and then --
PRESIDENT:  Pm or am?
MR TALANOV:  Evening, evening time, and the message, the
email that I received from him is 9.30.  That's when
the document arrived to our mailbox.
PRESIDENT:  Okay.  Thank you.
Any questions?  Yes.  Any questions?
We will resume in a few minutes.
(Short break)
PRESIDENT:  So the tribunal has deliberated and decided
not to grant respondent's application, so the document
is not allowed into the record.  It is a belated
application that does not comply with article 22 of
procedural order number 1.
MR TALANOV:  So could we clarify one thing?  It was not
actually the request for attaching the document, and
it was not therefore well reasoned and prepared.  It
was just the request for the guidance how to proceed
best.  So there was no request of the kind that has
now not been granted.  I mean --
PRESIDENT:  As to the presentation of evidence and the
introduction to evidence in this arbitration, the
rules are set forth in article 22.  So the tribunal
does not need to provide guidance to the parties.
Should a party wish to introduce a new evidence, it
has to be made in accordance with article 22 of P01,
unless the parties agree, confer and agree that the
document may be allowed into the record.
The tribunal at this point has no guidance or no
directions to give to the parties and any request for
or application to bring this document into the record
is belated because it does not comply with the
deadline set forth in article -- in procedural 21.
May I add that today, when we heard the
respondent, at no point in time did respondent explain
the reason why this document, which is contemporary to
the chronology of the facts on which the witnesses
will testify, was not introduced at an earlier stage
in the proceedings.  Having not provided any reason
why that could or could not have been brought to the
tribunal together with the witness statements or any
submission, on the morning of the hearing of the
relevant witnesses, there is no room for the tribunal
to provide any guidance to the parties.
And in any case, the record being closed, in order
to reopen the record there must be evidence provided
or arguments provided by the respondent that would
allow so that we provide both parties fairness in this
procedure and due process.
There is no reason that was provided for us to
allow the document in.
So both, on both grounds, no guidance is needed to
be provided by the tribunal at this stage, and the
document is not allowed into the record.  Thank you.
I hope this answers fully the application that was
made by the respondent.
MR TALANOV:  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  So we will now proceed with the evidentiary
hearing.  I suggest that -- I sent yesterday to the
parties a form.  I understand we're not in a common
law court.  Witnesses may not want to take oath, but
I would think that an affirmation of the truthfulness
of the witness evidence and testimony before this
tribunal, both in terms of fact witnesses and expert,
is something that is important for this tribunal.
So one way or another, I would ask, I would invite
the witness to read to the record an affirmation, and
we proposed a form to the parties that can be put in
front of the witness.  I will ask the witness to read
it for the record.
And then as far as direct examination is
concerned, we have reserved ten minutes.  And
I understand this will consist in confirming the
identity of the witness, the signature and -- of the
expert reports, and any additional correction or
additional points that may be made to the witness
statements.  But in terms of direct, we were provided
with several witness statements on both sides.  And
then we will turn to cross-examination.
This is how I think we should conduct, in
accordance with the timetable and procedural order
number 1 and 9, the examination of the witnesses.
But I see, counsel for claimant, you are about to
make a comment, so please go ahead.
MR HAUGENEDER:  We do have two points.  The first -- or
three points, actually.
First, we have printed your affirmation of truth
and we would, if you agree, put that in front of the
witness and the witness would read that into the
record.
As regards direct examination, our understanding
was that the ten minutes also serve to introduce a few
key elements of the testimony of the witness, so that
it is not just limited to an affirmation of the truth
and the confirmation of what's said in the witness
statements.  That was our understanding.  And then --
MR HOLLAND:  Members of the tribunal, yesterday, you
heard claimant's concerns about the integrity of the
arbitration and the admission of Mr Goeth.
We have since received the declaration of
confidentiality of Mr Goeth, and it is insufficient if
you consider the facts, in particular, that there is
another client of Mr Goeth's law firm that is
involved.  We may be able to put it on screen, but if
we cannot, the signed undertaking of Mr Goeth does
follow paragraph 71 of the tribunal's terms of
reference, which was from December 2022, but it
contains the agreed carve-out as follows:
"The disclosure of information is excused to the
extent that disclosure may be required by legal duty
or to protect or pursue a legal right or to enforce or
challenge an award in legal proceedings before a state
court or other legal authority."
So the difficulty here -- and this could not have
been anticipated, of course, by the tribunal or the
parties when the wording of that declaration of
confidentiality was agreed in 2023 in the terms of
reference -- is that now -- it's now on screen.  That
now, with the introduction to the competing client of
Mr Goeth's law firm, you will see from the second
bullet that the language of that second exclusion that
I just read out is now too broad.  It's overbroad.
It would include the right, the legal right
applying to Mr Goeth himself.  And that would include
any duties that were held by him and his law firm in
favour of the other client.
In other words, if it were necessary to pursue the
right of that client and not a party to these
proceedings, then that would make the undertaking
entirely useless.  And in fact, this was one of the
reasons that you heard us yesterday saying that we
felt that the admission of Mr Goeth would create
difficulties, professional and ethical, for him in
terms of conflicts of interest and for the other
participants.
Now, one solution would be to exclude and excuse
and delete that entire second --
PRESIDENT:  Bullet point.
MR HOLLAND:  The second bullet point would be --
PRESIDENT:  Just delete the entire sentence.
MR HOLLAND:  Yes.  And I think that that's justified
because the language of the terms of reference talks
about the signatories to the terms of reference, in
other words, the parties, the tribunal members.
We see no other solution to this because otherwise
it would be possible, in pursuit of the interests of
another client of the law firm of Mr Goeth, to do
almost anything with the documents and the decisions
made and these proceedings.
PRESIDENT:  Is your point, Mr Holland, that in order to
achieve confidentiality, the required confidentiality,
because this is not addressing 72.  This is not
addressing 72 of the terms of reference.  In order to
address confidentiality with respect to the parties
who are representative -- I mean, persons who are
representatives of the parties, we should delete
bullet number 2.
MR HOLLAND:  That's right.  I think it's 71.  72 was
a specific carve-out for Gazprom Export to tell its
parent company.
PRESIDENT:  Okay, I see.
MR HOLLAND:  But otherwise, yes, that is my submission.
And, I mean, in many countries it would be a conflict
of interest to be pursuing on the behalf of two
clients the limited, supposedly, resources of one
entity.  And there is a difficulty, I think, in that.
There is a conflict of interest in some ways between
the duties of the law firm in the hands of the client
and the party here.
PRESIDENT:  Let's hear from the respondent -- just to
make sure, Mr Goeth has not arrived yet?
MR TALANOV:  Mr Goeth is online.  He has connected
online.
PRESIDENT:  Can you please ask him to disconnect?
MR TALANOV:  Mr Goeth, could you please disconnect?
PRESIDENT:  I would very much -- parties to inform the
tribunal before the beginning of each day to indicate
who is attending online, so we can update the list of
participants.  So anyone from the respondent side who
is online and has not been introduced to the tribunal.
It is the duty of each party to introduce the
participants to the tribunal.
MR TALANOV:  Online from our side, we have Prof
Dr Hildebrand and Mr Philip Goeth, following the
exchange of the undertaking.
PRESIDENT:  Please ask Mr Philip Goeth --
MR TALANOV:  I have.
PRESIDENT:  -- to wait until the determination is made.
From the claimant's side, is there anyone online
the claimant would like to introduce at this stage?
No.  Thank you.
MS SOLDATENKOVA:  So in relation to the objection raised
by the other side, well, the wording follows precisely
the wording of the terms of reference.  For this
reason, the background for this objection is not
understood because it was part of the tribunal's
directions yesterday to reflect the same undertaking
as the parties undertook when they signed the terms of
reference.
In any event, the respondent is ready to consider
any alternative wording proposed by claimant.  But
I must emphasise that complete exclusion of
disclosures may be required by legal duty or to
protect or pursue a legal right, or to enforce or
challenge an award, maybe a carve-out that could
sometimes be contrary to the provisions of the
applicable law.  But we could consider such
a provision.
PRESIDENT:  Counsel, the wording of the directions of the
tribunal was twofold yesterday.  The first part was an
undertaking under the terms of reference for full
confidentiality, and another one was a declaration by
the new counsel that none of these undertakings
violate his duties or his law firm's duties towards
other clients and towards any court.
So the question is whether by deleting bullet
point number 2, we are actually erasing that
declaration.
It's very important to us that the counsel, the
new counsel, balances his own duties and is able to
make a declaration.  So if this declaration -- this
declaration is important to the tribunal and if,
balanced together with bullet number 2, it eviscerates
basically the declaration and the commitment by new
counsel, then the tribunal has concern and would have
to reconsider the terms of the admission of the new
counsel.
His undertaking is not limited to the terms of
reference, together with the exceptions to the terms
of reference.  It's very important that there is
additional undertaking made to the tribunal.
MS SOLDATENKOVA:  Madam chair, in this respect, what
I would suggest is, instead of deleting the second
bullet point, maybe what we could consider is
including a direct undertaking with respect to the
other clients to address the second part of the
concerns.  So the confidentiality concern is addressed
here in the text, and express wording, which would
address a concern in relation to his duties to the
other clients, could be addressed by the addition of
the point, probably below.
PRESIDENT:  Well, I think that declaration is already at
the bottom of the document.  It's already there.  The
question is the consistency between the second bullet
and the last paragraph.  So the application that the
claimant is making is to delete bullet point number 2.
And it's for Mr Goeth to determine whether he is able,
in view of its legal duties or the protection of any
legal right of its parties, to make the undertaking or
the declaration he's making at the bottom of the page.
So I think you have to confer with him before he's
admitted in.
MS SOLDATENKOVA:  Thank you.  We will discuss whether the
exclusion of the second bullet point would be
acceptable to address the concern fully.  Thank you.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.  Claimant?
MR HAUGENEDER:  Can we just clarify, whatever the
language that you will come up with is, there can be
no situation where Mr Goeth passes on confidential
information from this arbitration to the other client,
in whatever form, in whatever way.  And also if the
other client says he will keep it confidential.  So
that is not possible.  This arbitration is
confidential.  And if Mr Goeth believes that this is
necessary under his obligations as attorney of the
other client, then he simply cannot be counsel here.
That is the key.  That is the key concern from the
claimant.
If Mr Goeth says, I have duties as attorney
towards my other client and I need to inform him about
what has happened here because it is relevant for that
other client's matters, then obviously the
confidentiality of this arbitration would be breached,
and that is our concern.
PRESIDENT:  I think we heard your concern, that was
already addressed when you raised your objection, both
in writing and at the outset yesterday of the hearing.
And that concern was understood by the tribunal and
was addressed in the request the tribunal made that
Mr Goethe makes a declaration that this does not
violate any -- this confidentiality agreement does not
violate any of his duties to other parties or to the
court, or to any court.  So I think this point is
addressed in the last sentence.
MR HAUGENEDER:  I think we need to be careful about the
language that is used because passing on information
from this arbitration to the other client does
probably not violate any duties towards that other
client.  It breaches the confidentiality of this
arbitration.  And I think that that issue needs to be
addressed in the language that.
PRESIDENT:  And I think the remedy you're suggesting is
by deleting the second bullet point, right?
MR HAUGENEDER:  Meaning, and that must be the
understanding of everyone, that he cannot pass on
information from this arbitration to the other client.
PRESIDENT:  And again I'm asking you, if the second
bullet point is deleted from this document, does this
address the point of passing on information to another
party?
MR HAUGENEDER:  Yes, then that would be covered.
PRESIDENT:  And this is what will be reviewed by
Mr Goethe, and we will have the response.  I think you
need to confer with Mr Goethe on this point.
MR TALANOV:  I'm communicating with him right
immediately.  I think his proposal, I think that it
may be better addressing the concerns raised by the
claimant.
PRESIDENT:  Counsel, can you deal with this outside this
room with him so we can commence the evidentiary
hearing?
MR TALANOV:  Dear members of the tribunal, that is a very
strange situation, actually, so the party is not
having the chance to have the counsel that it wishes
to have on the substance of the case.  And we --
that's the second day that our counsel is not
accepted.  So, well, I understand that maybe that is
something --
PRESIDENT:  Counsel, may I interrupt you at this point?
Your new counsel was accepted yesterday before the
commencement of this hearing, subject to an
undertaking that was provided this morning.  So your
counsel has been admitted into this hearing promptly
by the tribunal at the outset of the hearing.
Now we are considering a document that was
provided by your counsel that is dated today -- not
yesterday -- and that for which the claimant has
concerns.  So this could have been addressed overnight
between the parties without taking the hearing time.
Now it is time.  There is an objection.  The
tribunal understands the objection, but would like
nonetheless to proceed with the evidentiary hearing,
so that we're not delayed by any commitments Mr Goeth
is making.
So if you or any member of your team want to
connect with him and provide to the tribunal
a revised, or an agreement on the concern addressed by
the claimant or any revised formulation, the tribunal
will examine it, but we will not suspend the
evidentiary hearing pending admission of Mr Goeth,
because Mr Goeth only provides this morning the
undertaking that was requested by the tribunal.
I understand he's intervening in this arbitration
as an expert on Austrian law.  I understand he's part
of the team, but the tribunal has to proceed with the
evidentiary hearing.
So we'll take a three-minute break and we'll
resume in three minutes, and we will commence the
evidentiary hearing.
At any point in time, if respondents provide us
with a document, we will review the document at any
break, and we will allow Mr Goeth.
But we cannot suspend this hearing because a new
counsel is coming to assist, and there is a concern as
to the undertaking that is made.  And the tribunal
wants to provide the integrity and the confidentiality
of these proceedings, and we want to best achieve this
by being provided with the undertaking that was
requested.  And if there is a concern on the wording,
then we need to review it.
So with this in mind, we have a three-minute break
and we resume at 10.18 and we will commence the
examination of the first witness.
(Short break)
MR PAVAO VUJNOVAC
PRESIDENT:  So we're back on record, and we will now
commence the evidentiary hearing.
Good morning, Mr Vujnovac.
WITNESS:  Good morning.
PRESIDENT:  Am I pronouncing your name correctly?
WITNESS:  Yes, yes.
PRESIDENT:  Please tell me, please correct me.
WITNESS:  No, no, no.  Yes.  You are pronouncing it
correct.
PRESIDENT:  Can you pronounce your own name so I --
WITNESS:  "Pavao Vujnovac".
PRESIDENT:  "Vujnovac", okay.
Mr Vujnovac, a very good morning to you and thank
you for coming to attend this hearing.  You are
a factual witness of the claimant in this arbitration.
The tribunal has been provided with the witness
statements you have submitted, your counsel has
submitted on behalf of the claimant in this
arbitration.
You will be asked questions of facts in the course
of your examination today, first by the claimant's
counsel and then by the respondent's counsel.
I would first ask you to read out loud to the
record the statement that is in front of you.  Do you
see it?
WITNESS:  Yes, yes.
PRESIDENT:  Please.
WITNESS:  So I, Pavao Vujnovac, do solemnly, sincerely
and truly declare and affirm that the evidence I shall
give shall be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing
but the truth.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you, sir.
I will now invite the claimant to have you affirm
your witness statements and conduct a direct that is
limited to ten minutes.
Examination-in-chief by MR HAUGENEDER
MR HAUGENEDER:  Thank you.
Good morning, Mr Vujnovac.  You have submitted two
witness statements in this arbitration.  Do you have
them in front of you?
A  Yes, yes.  Yes, it's here.
Q  Can you confirm the correctness of these witness
statements?
A  Yes, I can confirm.
Q  Do you wish to add or amend anything in your witness
statements?
A  No.
Q  Thank you.
Mr Vujnovac, you have signed a letter from Gazprom
dated 1 April 2022, which is well known to all
participants of this arbitration, in which Gazprom
requested to change the payment mechanism under the
supply contract.  Can you please explain why you
signed that letter?
A  So, when we received the letter, we were already in
a kind of, let's say stress, because the war already
started.  And I remember in 2009 when there was
a disruption of deliveries through Ukraine, at that
time I was leading PPD, which was a distribution
company.
And in 2009, when the disruptions happened, we
were shocked in Croatia, we had crisis procedures.
And at that time, we were shutting down deliveries to
practically all of the business customers except
households.  So we were going step by step.  And I saw
how the disruptions or a lack of supply can create
panic and disorder.  I think even today in Croatia, we
have lawsuits about 2009.
So when the war started, we were already in panic,
in a way, trying to see what the future will bring,
but nobody really understood what's going on.
And on 1 April, when I received the letter, I saw
that this is a step forward to the potential chaos,
because Central Eastern Europe, I mean, the area where
we are operating, was completely dependent on Gazprom
deliveries from the east, partially from Ukraine and
partially from the south stream.
It's still dependent because from the south it's
still coming, Russian gas through Serbia and Bulgaria.
And when I saw the letter, I was a bit in shock.
Croatia at that moment was very high on the list of
the enemies to the Russian State, I think we were
seventh or sixth, I'm not sure.  Me as a person, was
because of the former discussions and the price
review.  I didn't have the best image, plus Croatia
and so on, so I was very much afraid that they are
going to close down the contract.
So I saw that not signing the letter would be
a disaster.  Practically, we were -- I was dead or
alive.  So if I don't receive the gas and I had the
contracts towards the households, I was responsible
for complete security of supply of Croatia.
I didn't even reconsider not to sign under the
threat of cutting down supplies.
So I signed it before, because I thought I didn't
want to be the one which is not complying to the very
serious threat and that I'm -- that PPD would be
a kind of discussion somewhere that we are not signing
or really discussing or whatever, yeah?  So I wanted
to sign immediately so that the risk of not having
gas, we minimise.
So at the end I signed the letter on the 4th.
I was trying to reevaluate whether we should not do it
immediately or we should reconsider.  But the threat
was so strong and the alternatives of not getting gas
were practically no-go.
Q  Could you please explain why you didn't try to discuss
with Gazprom, why you immediately sent the
countersigned letter back?
A  Because they basically clearly stated there that it's
a kind of decree, I saw that also in the past, Gazprom
was very much in line with the Russian politics.  So
we saw also that this whole story was prepared much
longer period than one day.  We saw that decree was
brought 31 March.  They even sent the letter with all
the rules of Gazprombank, with all the, how to say,
informations about how we are going to comply.  They
have the whole model of the payments, and they clearly
said that if I don't sign they are going to cut off
deliveries.
So it was very, very clear in the letter and
I didn't want to be the one like under the spotlight
there, that I'm inside the war from Croatia, which is
an enemy country.  I'm somehow trying to rediscuss
some political decisions.
So I know that also from before, it was always
when Gazprom was signing contracts, this was always in
